description: A bit is a binary digit: 0 or 1. A byte is eight bits and can represent 256 distinct patterns. Text, images, and instructions are all stored as bits; the meaning comes from the encoding we agree on. CS50 Week 0 is the selected source for this representation idea. Do not complete the whole CS50 course.
title: Bits and bytes

description: Binary is base-2. Each place is a power of two. CS50 Week 0 covers unary, binary, and decimal. Practice converting values up to 8 bits by hand so the idea is automatic.
title: Binary

description: Hexadecimal is base-16. Each hex digit is exactly four bits, so 1111 is F and a byte is two hex digits. CS50 Week 0 teaches binary/decimal; hex is the same positional idea with grouping. You will see hex in memory dumps, color codes (#RRGGBB), and addresses.
title: Hexadecimal

description: The CPU (central processing unit) fetches instructions and data, decodes them, and executes them. It is not the same as RAM (working memory) or disk (persistent storage). CS50 does not teach a full computer-architecture course; this lesson is the internal explanation. Week 1 still helps: source becomes machine code that a processor can run.
title: CPU

description: The ALU (arithmetic logic unit) is the part of the CPU that performs integer arithmetic and boolean operations (add, subtract, AND, OR, compare). High-level expressions like `x + 1` and `a && b` become ALU operations after compilation. This topic has no selected CS50 lecture that names the ALU; the lesson is the explanation.
title: ALU

description: Registers are tiny, extremely fast storage locations inside the CPU. They hold the instruction being worked on, addresses, and intermediate results. There are few of them, so the CPU constantly moves data between registers and RAM. No CS50 week is a register-file course; this is an internal explanation.
title: Registers

description: RAM (main memory) holds the running program's code and data. It is volatile: contents disappear when power is gone. It is larger and slower than registers, smaller and faster than disk. A program on disk is not executing until loaded.
title: RAM

description: A cache is a small fast memory that stores recently used data and instructions so the CPU does not wait on RAM every time. It works because programs reuse nearby data (locality). You do not need cache-coherence protocols at this level.
title: Cache

description: Storage (SSD/HDD) keeps data when power is off. It is slower than RAM. Files, installed programs, and Git repos live here. The OS copies needed pieces into RAM to run them.
title: Storage

description: The processor repeats: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode what it means, execute it (often with the ALU), then continue. A simple assignment becomes several instructions. CS50 Week 1 shows source becoming machine code; it does not walk microarchitecture pipelines.
title: Instruction execution

description: Machine code is the binary instruction encoding a CPU family can execute. It is architecture-specific. CS50 Week 1: source code is compiled to machine code you can run.
title: Machine code

description: A compiler translates source into machine code or bytecode before the program runs (compile time vs run time). CS50 Week 1 is the selected primary: clang/make turning .c into a runnable file.
title: Compiler

description: An interpreter executes a program by analyzing and running it incrementally (or running bytecode on a VM). You often need the language runtime installed. CS50 Week 1 is compiler-centric; this lesson supplies the contrast. Python is a familiar interpreted/VM example you may already know from C++-adjacent tooling.
title: Interpreter

description: A program is an artifact: source, maybe compiled form, sitting on storage. It is not yet a running process. CS50 Week 1 treats .c and the executable as program forms.
title: Program

description: A process is the OS's running instance of a program: its own memory space, open files, and identity (PID). The same program can have many processes. MIT Missing Semester's shell lecture shows the shell starting programs; it is not a full OS textbook.
title: Process

description: The kernel is the privileged program that manages hardware, processes, memory, and filesystems. User programs ask it for services via system calls. Missing Semester is not an OS course; this explanation is the lesson.
title: Kernel

description: The OS creates, schedules, and isolates processes. Each process has an identity and resources.
title: Processes

description: Threads are multiple execution paths inside one process and share that process's memory. CS50 Week 0 mentions threads in Scratch as a light analogy only.
title: Threads

description: A system call is how a user program asks the kernel to do privileged work such as reading a file or creating a process.
title: System calls

description: Each process has an address space. The OS allocates pages and protects regions.
title: Memory

description: Virtual memory lets each process see its own address space. The OS maps virtual pages to physical frames or swap.
title: Virtual memory basics

description: A filesystem presents files and directories on storage. Paths name them. The kernel enforces structure and permissions.
title: Filesystems

description: Unix permission bits say who may read, write, or execute a file. The kernel enforces them.
title: Permissions

description: Environment variables are key-value settings inherited by child processes (PATH, HOME).
title: Environment variables

description: The shell reads commands and starts programs. Bash/Zsh are Unix shells. Windows users must use WSL or a Linux VM. PowerShell is a different ecosystem, not the target.
title: Shell

description: Commands have a name, arguments, flags, stdin/stdout/stderr, and an exit status. Official MIT exercises cover quoting, exit codes, and conditionals.
title: Command line

description: pwd, ls, and cd are the core navigation tools. Relative vs absolute paths. MIT shell lecture is primary.
title: Filesystem navigation

description: touch, cp, mv, rm, mkdir, rmdir. Be careful with rm. Official MIT exercises include executable files and scripts.
title: Files

description: A pipe connects stdout of one process to stdin of the next. MIT lecture introduces pipes; official exercises include pipelines.
title: Pipes

description: >, >>, 2>, < attach files to standard streams. Official MIT exercise: redirect stdout and stderr separately.
title: Redirection

description: grep finds lines matching a pattern. MIT lecture uses grep in pipelines (curl | grep). man grep is the reference.
title: grep

description: find walks a tree. Official MIT exercises combine find with globs, xargs, and -mtime.
title: find

description: Apply OS permission concepts at the terminal: ls -l, chmod, executable scripts. Official MIT chmod exercise.
title: Permissions

description: ps lists processes. You already used it conceptually; now do it as a skill. man ps is the reference.
title: Processes

description: OS package managers install/update software with dependency tracking. MIT command-line lecture names apt/brew; shipping lecture goes deeper on language packaging.
title: Package management

description: export, printenv, PATH. Builds on OS environment variables with hands-on shell skill. MIT CLI lecture covers customization.
title: Environment variables

description: A Git repository stores snapshots of a project in .git. git init or git clone. Pro Git 2.1 is canonical.
title: Repository

description: Staging selects what goes into the next snapshot. Commits record it. Why staging exists: craft the snapshot.
title: Commits

description: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. Parallel lines of work.
title: Branches

description: Merge joins histories. Fast-forward vs merge commit. Canonical: Basic Branching and Merging.
title: Merge

description: Rebase replays commits on a new base. Do not rebase shared published branches. Practice only locally in V1.
title: Rebase

description: origin is a conventional remote name. git remote -v lists URLs.
title: Remote

description: fetch downloads; merge/rebase integrates; pull is fetch+integrate. push sends. Use official docs, not blog search pages.
title: Pull and push

description: Conflicts happen when both sides edit the same lines. Markers <<<<<< ====== >>>>>>. Pro Git merge conflict section.
title: Conflicts

description: reset moves a branch pointer; revert adds a new undoing commit (safe for published history); restore adjusts files. Canonical pages.
title: Reset and revert

description: Cherry-pick copies a commit. Official git-cherry-pick(1).
title: Cherry-pick

description: stash saves dirty work and restores a clean tree. Book + git-stash(1).
title: Stash

description: GitHub Hello World: repository → branch → commit → pull request → merge. Use a private repo you own.
title: GitHub workflow

description: An IDE combines editor, run/debug, and project tools. VS Code is what you use day to day, but the skill is using one well. PRIMARY structured course for this module is TBD — do not treat a random YouTube playlist as a substitute. MIT 2026 development-environment lecture is Vim-heavy; it still defines what a development environment is.
title: IDE

description: Apply cf-compiler in a real toolchain. You may not have javac yet; recording versions of gcc/clang/python still counts. PRIMARY course TBD.
title: Compiler

description: Stepping beats printf-only debugging. VS Code debugger docs are official. MIT debugging lecture is Unix/gdb-oriented and useful as extra depth.
title: Debugger

description: Formatters apply a consistent style. MIT Code Quality covers formatters. VS Code can format the current file.
title: Formatter

description: Linters are static hints. MIT Code Quality. Not the same as a compiler error.
title: Linter

description: npm/Maven/pip vs apt/brew. MIT shipping-code is the verified lecture for artifacts and language packages.
title: Package manager

description: Compile + test + package as a repeatable pipeline. make in CS50 Week 1; command runners in MIT Code Quality.
title: Build system

description: Direct deps you declare; transitive come in with them. Risks: breakage, supply chain. MIT shipping lecture.
title: Dependency management

description: CS50 Week 0: inputs, outputs, computational thinking. Split before coding.
title: Problem decomposition

description: CS50 Week 0 covers pseudocode. Syntax-free thinking.
title: Pseudocode

description: CS50 Week 0: algorithms and running times. Algorithm vs program.
title: Algorithms

description: Manual execution before trusting code. Table of variable values per step.
title: Dry runs

description: Inputs that break naive solutions: empty, one element, duplicates, already sorted, huge.
title: Edge cases

description: Observe, hypothesize, test. MIT debugging lecture + CS50 correctness. Do not randomly edit.
title: Debugging

description: CS50 Week 0 running times. O(n) vs O(n^2) as input grows. No recurrences.
title: Time complexity introduction

description: O(1) extra space vs O(n) extra arrays. First contact only.
title: Space complexity introduction

description: The JDK (Java Development Kit) is what you install to compile and run Java. The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) executes bytecode. A JRE was historically a runtime-only subset; modern OpenJDK/Oracle distributions emphasize the JDK. You write .java source, javac (or the Java launcher) produces .class bytecode, and the JVM runs it. Helsinki's setup still mentions older NetBeans/TMC tooling — that is not required. Verify `java -version` and `javac -version` on your machine. IDE choice is optional (VS Code is fine).
title: JDK and JRE

description: A first Java application is a class with `public static void main(String[] args)`. The file name should match the public class. Printing uses System.out. Starting with recent JDKs you can also launch a `.java` source file directly; still learn the class/main shape because DSA and interviews expect it. Do not complete Helsinki as a beginner-from-zero course — use the first print exercises as reps.
title: First program

description: javac compiles source to bytecode (.class). java launches the JVM against a class name (not the .java file name with extension, unless you use source-file mode). Modern JDKs can run `java Hello.java` for simple programs. You still need to understand classpath and that the launcher loads classes. This compile-run loop is the tooling for the rest of Java and for running DSA solutions.
title: Compile and run

description: Java primitives are boolean, byte, short, int, long, float, double, and char. They are not objects. String is a reference type (a class), even though it has literals. `var` infers a type from the initializer; it is not a dynamic type. Uninitialized local variables cannot be read. Prefer explicit types while learning; use var when the type is obvious.
title: Primitives

description: Widening conversions (int → long → float → double) can be implicit. Narrowing (double → int, long → int) needs a cast and can truncate. Integer overflow wraps in two's complement; it does not throw. Mixing int division (`5 / 2`) truncates. Boxing (int ↔ Integer) is separate from primitive widening — see autoboxing later when you use collections.
title: Type conversion

description: Console programs write with System.out (print/printf) and read with java.util.Scanner or similar. Always validate: empty lines, non-numeric text, and out-of-range values. Do not obsess over Scanner internals. Helsinki Part 1 reading exercises are the practice layer. Build a tiny CLI: prompt → parse → compute → repeat until quit.
title: Console input and output

description: Operators combine values. Precedence and associativity matter; when unclear, use parentheses. `&&` and `||` short-circuit: the right operand may not run. `++i` vs `i++` differs when the value is used in a larger expression. The ternary `cond ? a : b` is an expression. Assignment is `=`; equality is `==` (for primitives).
title: Operators

description: if/else chooses a path from a boolean. Nesting is legal but deep nesting is a smell — extract methods or invert conditions. Brace style: always use braces for bodies you will maintain. Helsinki conditionals are the exercise set.
title: if/else

description: Classic switch statements jump on a discrete value and historically needed break to avoid fall-through. Modern switch expressions (`switch (x) { case 1 -> "a"; default -> "b"; }`) yield a value and do not fall through. Helsinki predates much of this: treat Dev.java as authoritative. Do not memorize every preview feature; statements vs expressions is the core.
title: switch

description: while tests before the body; do-while tests after (body runs at least once); for combines init/test/update. Enhanced for comes with arrays/collections. Helsinki repeating + more-loops is the exercise battery. Pattern printing is fine as motor practice; prefer problems with a stopping condition you can state in words.
title: Loops

description: break leaves the innermost loop or switch. continue skips the rest of this iteration. Labeled break exists but is rarely the clearest design. Prefer a boolean condition when it reads better.
title: break and continue

description: A method has a name, parameter list, return type (or void), and body. Callers pass arguments. Java is pass-by-value: primitives are copied; for objects, the reference value is copied, so the callee can mutate the same object but cannot make the caller's variable point elsewhere. DSA connection: after this topic, Domain 2 may depend on Java methods. Streams, lambdas, concurrency, and JVM topics are not DSA gates.
title: Method basics

description: Overloading: same name, different parameter types or arity. The compiler picks the best match. You cannot overload on return type only. Constructors can overload too (next OOP module). Do not confuse with overriding (runtime, inheritance).
title: Overloading

description: A local variable lives from its declaration to the end of its block. Parameters are locals. Fields (later) live as long as the object. Nested blocks can shadow. Loops' for-init variables are scoped to the loop.
title: Scope

description: A Java array has a fixed length after creation. Indices are 0..length-1. `arr[i]` is O(1) access. The variable holds a reference; assignment copies the reference (aliasing). Multidimensional arrays are arrays of arrays. Out-of-bounds throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Do not turn this into the DSA arrays module: min/max/reverse/rotate/prefix-sum here are language fluency. DSA connection: Domain 2 array patterns (traversal, two pointers, prefix sums) use this language foundation. This topic is Java arrays, not the DSA module. C++ analogue: T[] is closer to a fixed buffer than std::vector (vector ≈ ArrayList later).
title: Arrays

description: String objects are immutable: concatenation builds a new String. Compare content with equals, not == (== is reference identity; interned literals can make == accidentally 'work'). charAt, substring, toCharArray, split, and Character methods cover most interview string work. DSA connection: Domain 2 string problems use Java String and character processing.
title: Strings

description: StringBuilder is a mutable sequence. append/insert/delete mutate the same object. It is not thread-safe (StringBuffer is the older synchronized cousin; you do not need it here). Use String for immutable values and APIs; StringBuilder for loops that assemble text.
title: StringBuilder

description: A class is the blueprint; an object is an instance. Fields hold state; methods are behavior. `new` allocates and runs a constructor. `this` is the current instance. Access control starts here (public/private) and continues in encapsulation. Build small domain models (Student, Book), not CRUD apps. DSA connection: linked lists, trees, and graphs in Domain 2 depend on classes plus reference/aliasing semantics.
title: Classes and objects

description: A reference variable holds either null or an identity of an object. Assignment `a = b` copies the reference. Mutating through either name changes the one object. Rebinding `a = new ...` does not change b. This is the mental model for linked lists, trees, and graphs. Java is not pass-by-reference. DSA connection: linked lists, trees, and graphs in Domain 2 depend on classes plus reference/aliasing semantics. Java is pass-by-value; the value copied for objects is the reference.
title: References

description: Constructors initialize new objects. They have no return type. You can overload them. `this(...)` must be the first statement when chaining. If you write any constructor, Java does not supply the default no-arg one.
title: Constructors

description: Encapsulation: keep fields private and expose a small API that preserves invariants (balance >= 0). Getters/setters are not mandatory boilerplate. A public setter that allows any value destroys the invariant. Prefer immutable fields when mutation is not part of the domain.
title: Encapsulation

description: extends creates an is-a relationship. Subclasses inherit accessible members, override methods, and chain constructors with super(). protected is for subclass access. Inheritance is not the default design tool: a fragile hierarchy is worse than composition. After the exercise, answer: would composition be better?
title: Inheritance

description: The compile-time type of a variable decides which members you can name. The runtime class of the object decides which override runs (dynamic dispatch). Interface types work the same way. instanceof (and pattern matching) tests runtime type — use sparingly vs real polymorphism. Not a DSA gate, but it shows up in Java design.
title: Polymorphism

description: An abstract class cannot be instantiated. Abstract methods force subclasses to implement. Use an abstract class when you have shared fields/implementation plus holes to fill. Prefer interfaces for capability types (Payable, Comparable) — next topic.
title: Abstract classes

description: An interface is a contract. A class implements it. Variables can have the interface type (dependency inversion intro: depend on PaymentProcessor, not StripeProcessor). Default methods add library evolution; static methods are helpers on the interface. Multiple interfaces are allowed; multiple class inheritance is not. Connects to later backend: storage, notifications, payment.
title: Interfaces

description: Composition: an object holds another (Car has Engine, Order has List<Line>). This is the usual has-a tool and often beats inheritance. Helsinki 'objects within objects' plus 'separate UI from logic' is the practical story. For DSA, a Graph composes lists/maps of nodes; it should not extend HashMap.
title: Composition

description: Exceptions signal that a method cannot complete normally. try/catch handles a specific type you can recover from. finally runs for cleanup. Prefer try-with-resources for Closeable I/O (File I/O module). Do not catch Exception everywhere. Empty catch blocks hide bugs.
title: try/catch

description: Unchecked: RuntimeException and Error — compiler does not require catch/throws (NPE, IAE, IOBE). Checked: other Exception subclasses — callers must catch or declare throws (classic IOException). APIs disagree on how much checked is good; don't invent checked exceptions for every domain miss. Propagation: if you cannot handle it, declare throws or wrap.
title: Checked and unchecked

description: A custom exception is a type that names a domain failure (InsufficientFundsException). Extend RuntimeException unless you have a strong reason for checked. Include a message and optionally a cause. Throw at the boundary; don't use exceptions for normal returns.
title: Custom exceptions

description: List is an ordered Collection. ArrayList is a resizable array (C++ vector). LinkedList is a doubly linked list — rarely the default. Program to List, construct ArrayList. Indexing ArrayList is O(1); adding at the end is amortized O(1). Helsinki Part 3 lists are ArrayList-heavy. DSA connection: ArrayList is the usual Java stand-in for a resizable array / C++ vector. Domain 2 stack/queue topics still need classes + references; List is the usual Java backbone.
title: List

description: Set stores unique elements. HashSet is average O(1) add/contains (C++ unordered_set). Iteration order is not a contract unless you use LinkedHashSet/TreeSet. Elements must have consistent equals/hashCode. Helsinki maps uniqueness more via HashMap; Dev.java Set is the reference. DSA connection: HashSet is used heavily for uniqueness and hashing problems. C++ analogue: unordered_set.
title: Set

description: Map stores key → value. HashMap is average O(1) get/put (C++ unordered_map). Keys need equals/hashCode. Frequency maps (char → int) and adjacency maps (node → list) are Domain 2 workhorses. getOrDefault, merge, and iterate entrySet. Null keys: HashMap allows one null key; don't rely on it in DSA. DSA connection: HashMap is used heavily for hashing, frequency, and graphs. C++ analogue: unordered_map.
title: Map

description: Enhanced for uses Iterable. Iterator has hasNext/next/remove. Do not remove from an ArrayList while enhanced-for iterating (ConcurrentModificationException). Use Iterator.remove or iterate indices carefully. index loops remain valid for arrays and when you need the index.
title: Iteration

description: PriorityQueue is a heap: poll gives the least element by natural or Comparator order (head is the smallest by default). It is not a sorted list — only the head is cheap. ArrayDeque is the usual queue/stack (C++ deque). C++ priority_queue is the analogue of PriorityQueue (and is a max-heap by default — Java's is min-heap by Comparable). DSA connection: heaps in Domain 2 use PriorityQueue plus Comparable/Comparator. C++ analogue: priority_queue. Streams are not required.
title: PriorityQueue

description: Generics parameterize types: Box<T>, List<String>. They exist for compile-time type safety. At runtime, type erasure means the JVM sees raw types (conceptual level only). Do not overteach PECS yet — next topic. Helsinki Part 12 type parameters is the exercise layer.
title: Generic types

description: T extends Number restricts T. Wildcards: List<?> unknown, List<? extends Number> producer, List<? super Integer> consumer (PECS at slogan level). You need to read these in APIs. You do not need to invent nested wildcards for DSA.
title: Bounds

description: Comparable.compareTo is the type's natural order. Comparator is an external strategy (multiple criteria, reverse). Collections.sort / List.sort / PriorityQueue use these. Lambda: Comparator.comparing(Person::age).thenComparing(Person::name). DSA connection: heaps in Domain 2 use PriorityQueue plus Comparable/Comparator. C++ analogue: priority_queue.
title: Comparable and Comparator

description: A functional interface has one abstract method (SAM). @FunctionalInterface documents that. Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, Comparator are the workhorses. This is practical Java, not category theory. Not a DSA prerequisite.
title: Functional interfaces

description: Lambda: (args) -> body. Captured locals must be effectively final. Method references (String::length) are shorthand. Use them with List.sort, Iterable.forEach, and later Streams. Not a DSA prerequisite.
title: Lambdas

description: A Stream is not a data structure and not an I/O stream. Source → intermediate (lazy) → terminal (eager, consumes). You can use a pipeline only once. Prefer stateless, side-effect-free intermediates. Not a DSA prerequisite.
title: Stream pipeline

description: map transforms, filter keeps, reduce/collect aggregates. groupingBy builds maps. sorted uses Comparator. Optional appears as findFirst. Keep pipelines readable; don't golf. Not a DSA prerequisite.
title: Common operations

description: java.nio.file.Path locates a file. Files has helpers: exists, readString, writeString, newBufferedReader. Handle missing files with exceptions or exists checks. This is NIO.2, not the Stream API. Helsinki file parts may show older File/Scanner styles — prefer Path/Files in new code.
title: Paths and files

description: Character streams (Reader/Writer) handle text. Byte streams (InputStream/OutputStream) handle bytes. Buffering matters for performance. try-with-resources closes them. This is I/O, not java.util.stream.Stream.
title: Readers and writers

description: A unit test checks one behavior of a method with a clear name. JUnit runs methods annotated @Test. Tests should be independent. Helsinki introduces testing; JUnit 5 docs are the modern runner reference. This is not a full testing-career course.
title: JUnit basics

description: assertEquals, assertTrue, assertThrows check outcomes. Test boundaries (0, empty, max). Java's `assert` keyword is a different, usually-off mechanism — do not confuse it with JUnit. Write tests before or after implementation; the point is the spec.
title: Assertions

description: A process is an OS program instance. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process sharing memory. Runnable is the task; Thread/Executor runs it. ExecutorService is the modern default over raw new Thread. Virtual threads (Dev.java) are a modern scaling feature — reference only, not a DSA gate. Helsinki does not map to a verified concurrency part here.
title: Threads

description: A race: two threads update shared mutable state with no happens-before. synchronized / locks make a critical section. Visibility: without synchronization, another thread may never see your write. Concurrent collections exist; don't roll a concurrent HashMap by hand. Not a DSA algorithms course.
title: Synchronization basics

description: javac emits bytecode in .class files. The JVM loads classes and executes bytecode (then JIT may compile hot methods to native). javap -c disassembles. You do not need to memorize opcodes.
title: Bytecode

description: Each method call has a stack frame (locals, including references). Objects live on the heap (programmer model). The Java Memory Model also defines visibility between threads — you saw that in synchronization. There is no dedicated Dev.java 'heap vs stack' chapter; this is an internal lesson plus GC as heap context. Not JVM internals / not a DSA gate.
title: Memory model basics

description: Garbage collection frees heap objects that are not reachable from GC roots (stacks, statics, etc.). You don't call free(). Memory leaks in Java are usually accidental retained references. Tuning collectors is out of scope. Profiling awareness: jcmd/JFR exist; you don't need them daily yet.
title: Garbage collection intro

description: Packages are namespaces that match directory structure. com.example.util.Strings lives in com/example/util/Strings.java. import names types; wildcard imports are optional. Not a DSA prerequisite.
title: Packages

description: Professional Java: clear names, small methods, immutability where it helps, no Spring Boot yet. Maven (Helsinki Part 14) or Gradle builds, tests, and dependencies. Format/lint in the editor. Logging > println in apps; debugger > guess-and-print. Code review is reading diffs for intent. Records/modules/virtual threads stay reference — not required here.
title: API hygiene

description: You already know DSA in C++. This is a rebuild of fundamentals for Java interviews and deeper reasoning, not a first course in programming. Algorithmic thinking is language-independent: define input and output, write two small examples (including an edge case), state an invariant or brute-force sketch, then choose a structure. You already decompose problems in C++; Java is the interview implementation language. Implement in Java. C++ is an equivalence note, not a second curriculum. Watching Abdul Bari or MIT lectures clarifies vocabulary — it is not mastery.
title: Algorithmic thinking

description: You already know DSA in C++. This is a rebuild of fundamentals for Java interviews and deeper reasoning, not a first course in programming. Big-O describes asymptotic growth: constant factors and lower terms drop out. Count dominant operations in loops — one loop over n is O(n), nested loops often O(n²). This formalizes Domain 0's complexity intro. Same reasoning in C++ and Java. Watching Time Complexity / Asymptotic Notation lectures is not mastery.
title: Big-O notation

description: You already know DSA in C++. This is a rebuild of fundamentals for Java interviews and deeper reasoning, not a first course in programming. The same algorithm can differ by input shape: quicksort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst on bad pivots. HashMap lookup is O(1) average but degrades with many collisions. Interviews usually ask worst-case unless stated otherwise. Abdul Bari's Frequency Count / analysis lectures and MIT L19 deepen this — not mastery alone.
title: Best, worst, average

description: You already know DSA in C++. This is a rebuild of fundamentals for Java interviews and deeper reasoning, not a first course in programming. Traversal is index-driven linear scan: forward, backward, or with a step. Java int[] / ArrayList ≈ C++ vector (ArrayList grows; raw arrays are fixed). Use enhanced for when you only need values; use index loops when you need i or in-place writes. No Domain 1 array syntax lesson — focus on algorithmic scans.
title: Array traversal

description: You already know DSA in C++. This is a rebuild of fundamentals for Java interviews and deeper reasoning, not a first course in programming. Contiguous arrays shift elements on middle insert/delete — O(n) worst case. ArrayList append is amortized O(1); insert at index i costs O(n-i). Java int[] / ArrayList ≈ C++ vector (ArrayList grows; raw arrays are fixed). Same shifting intuition as C++ vector.
title: Insertion and deletion concepts

description: You already know DSA in C++. This is a rebuild of fundamentals for Java interviews and deeper reasoning, not a first course in programming. prefix[i] = sum(a[0..i]). Range l..r = prefix[r] - prefix[l-1] (l=0 → prefix[r]). O(n) build, O(1) query — same prefix array technique as C++.
title: Prefix sums

description: You already know DSA in C++. This is a rebuild of fundamentals for Java interviews and deeper reasoning, not a first course in programming. Small fixed domain → int[26], int[10], etc. O(1) update per element. Graduate to HashMap when keys are large or unbounded. Same counting array idea as C++.
title: Frequency counting

description: You already know DSA in C++. This is a rebuild of fundamentals for Java interviews and deeper reasoning, not a first course in programming. Patterns: compaction with write index, opposite pointers on sorted data, partition reorder. Foundation for two pointers and sliding window modules.
title: Array patterns

description: You already know DSA in C++. This is a rebuild of fundamentals for Java interviews and deeper reasoning, not a first course in programming. Java String is immutable; StringBuilder ≈ C++ string mutation. Do not redo Domain 1 syntax. DSA focus: index walks, substring views, two-pointer on chars. Use StringBuilder for assembly in loops — not a Domain 1 syntax lesson.
title: String manipulation

description: You already know DSA in C++. This is a rebuild of fundamentals for Java interviews and deeper reasoning, not a first course in programming. Character frequency drives anagrams, permutations-in-window, and multiset comparisons. int[26] or HashMap depending on alphabet — same counting logic as C++.
title: String frequency
